archetype.name: Playoff Team (riding the percentages)
archetype.definition: A Boston side that genuinely out-chances teams at 5-on-5 and has elite goaltending, but whose league-best goal margin is inflated by finishing and save rates far above anything that holds over 82 games.

report.headline: Real improvement under the hood, but the 130-point pace is mostly percentages
report.take:
Boston sits first on the site at 9-2-1 with the league's best goal differential per game (1.83), a top-three offense and a top-two defense. That reads like a juggernaut. The underlying shape is more modest. The Bruins rank 23rd in Shots / GP (26.3) and 20th in Shots Against / GP (27.8), and their CF % is .49, 17th. They are not dictating possession. They are winning because nearly everything they shoot goes in and nearly everything against them stays out.

The percentages are the story. Skaters are shooting 15.2% in all situations against a league average of 11.3%, and the goalies are stopping .925 against a league .892. Together that makes a PDO of 107.8 in all situations, first in the league, and 107.6 at 5-on-5, 7.6 above average. Swayman (.920, 6.1 GSAx, third on the goalie tab) and DiPietro (.941 in three starts) have combined for a league-best 10.9 Goalies GSAx. Up front, Pastrnak's 17 points lead a forward group graded A+ that has unusual depth at center: Minten, Elias Lindholm and Hagens all sit between 25th and 27th on a 230-man tab.

The numbers also hide some real progress, which separates this from a pure mirage. Boston's xGF % is .553, sixth in the league. Last season it was .473 and the year before .484, so the Bruins are generating a better share of quality chances at 5-on-5 than at any point in this history. Their record isn't flattered by close-game luck either. Pts vs Goal Diff is -0.9, 24th, so the standings are, if anything, slightly behind the goal margin. And last year's 100-point team also leaned on goaltending, with 30.6 GSAx, so the save-percentage edge has some track record behind it.

The direction from here is a good team coming back to earth, not a collapse. The 62-win, 130-point pace will not survive a shooting percentage drifting back toward the league norm. A shot-share team near 50% with a chance-share near 55% and a strong goalie tandem is still a comfortable playoff side and a plausible division winner. The ceiling depends on whether the xGF gain is real enough to cover for finishing that cools.

trend.note: Two flat losses to Minnesota and Ottawa in early October gave way to a dominant run. The last five games went 4-0-1, outscoring opponents 22-10, with goals per game up 0.4 on the season average.

weekAhead.headline: Carolina tests the shot gap; Chicago and St. Louis offer cushion
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with the hardest game on the calendar. Boston visits Carolina, second on the site and the league's top shot generator at 33.9 a game, with a CF % of .59. That is the matchup most likely to expose Boston's below-average shot share. It may come down to whether Swayman can outduel a Hurricanes crease graded only C. A trip to St. Louis follows, a .500-ish 20th-ranked team whose defense has been among the league's worst against centers.

The homestand is friendlier. Chicago (3-8-0, 31st) ranks 30th or worse in goals for, goals against, xGF % and CF %, and owns the league's worst power play at 8.3%. Vegas (8-4-1, 11th) is the stronger closer, with a good xGF % of .546. But its PK % of .677 ranks 28th and its goaltending carries a D+ grade, so Boston's power play and finishers should get their looks. Three of four games are against teams with weaker goaltending grades than Boston's.

keyMatchups.title: Hurricanes' shot volume versus Boston's crease
keyMatchups.body: Carolina leads the league in shots per game, while Boston allows the 20th-most. The Bruins have survived being out-shot because their goalies lead the league in GSAx. This road game is where that dependence is most visible.

keyMatchups.title: Center depth against soft middles
keyMatchups.body: St. Louis ranks 31st and Chicago 30th in points allowed to centers relative to expectation. That plays directly into Boston's deepest position, with Minten, Lindholm and Hagens all ranked among the top 27 centers on the site.

keyMatchups.title: Boston power play versus Vegas kill
keyMatchups.body: Vegas kills penalties at 67.7%, 28th in the league. Boston's power play is above average at 22.2%, and Pastrnak alone has five PP points. Special teams could decide what looks like the week's closest home game.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Boston can hold its own in shot attempts at Carolina, the best possession team on the schedule, rather than relying on the goalie to bail it out.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect the goal margin to shrink noticeably. A 15.2% team shooting rate and a .925 save percentage are both far above league norms, and the shot counts behind them are below average. The finishing edge is the part most likely to fade. The goaltending edge should partly hold, given last season's 30.6 GSAx. What should last is the improved chance share: a .553 xGF % is a legitimate top-ten mark, and the forward group has depth. Boston also hasn't been lucky in close games, which removes one common source of regression.

The realistic landing spot is a 102-114 point season with something like 47-53 wins. That would be an improvement on last year's 100 points, but nowhere near the current 130-point pace. Goals for should settle somewhere around 3.2-3.6 a game as shooting cools, with goals against creeping up toward 2.6-2.9.
swingFactors: How far team shooting % falls from 15.2%
Whether the .553 xGF % holds against better opponents

confidence.note: Only 12 games played, with record-high percentages. But the xGF % and goaltending history give real signal.
